title: Who Is Sethuraman Panchanathan? The Chennai-Born Scientist Who Ran the NSF — and Just Became the First Indian American to Win Engineering's Bueche Award
excerpt: He queued in Chennai at age eight to see Apollo 11's moon rocks and decided the ingenuity mattered more than the stones. Fifty-seven years later, Sethuraman 'Panch' Panchanathan — 15th director of the National Science Foundation, Padma Shri recipient — has received the National Academy of Engineering's highest policy honour, an award no Indian American had won in its 43 years.
body:
• Sethuraman Panchanathan, the Chennai-born computer scientist who served as the 15th director of the U.S. National Science Foundation from 2020 to 2025, received the National Academy of Engineering's 2026 Arthur M. Bueche Award on October 4 in Washington, D.C.
  • He is the first Indian American — and the first Arizonan — to win the Bueche Award in its more than 40-year history, honoured for leadership in science and technology policy and for expanding research opportunity nationwide.
  • His career runs in one line: four degrees across India and Canada, 28 years at Arizona State University, the creation of the NSF's first new directorate in more than 30 years, and a Padma Shri from India in 2025.
  • For the diaspora, his signature argument is now institutional fact: talent is everywhere, opportunity is not — and he spent five years running America's basic-research funder trying to close that gap, including through formal research partnerships with India.

On October 4, 2026, the National Academy of Engineering presented its Arthur M. Bueche Award to an engineer who first decided science was his life's work while standing in a queue in Chennai, aged eight, waiting to look at some grey pebbles. Sethuraman Panchanathan — "Panch" to the American science establishment he has inhabited for three decades — became the first Indian American, and the first Arizonan, to receive the award in its more than 40-year history, according to Arizona State University. The Bueche Award, established in 1983, does not honour a single discovery. It honours an engineer for "active involvement in determining U.S. science and technology policy, promoting technological development, and contributing to the enhancement of the relationship between industries, government and universities." That is a precise description of Panchanathan's career.

The Academy's citation credits him "for leadership in promoting fundamental science, technology and policy that advances translational research and expands opportunities nationwide." He received the award 17 months after stepping down as the 15th director of the National Science Foundation, the roughly $9 billion federal agency that funds basic research across every field of science and engineering in the United States, and a year after India gave him the Padma Shri. Few living scientists have been decorated at the top level by both countries. Panchanathan, 65, is now one of them.

"The rocks were just rocks. But what fascinated me was all the human ingenuity and scientific prowess that went into bringing them here."

— Sethuraman Panchanathan, on seeing the Apollo 11 moon rocks in Chennai in 1969

Chennai, moon rocks, and four degrees

Panchanathan was born on June 24, 1961, in Chennai. In 1969 his father took him to the American Center in the city, where rocks brought back by Apollo 11 were on public display. The stones underwhelmed him; the achievement behind them did not. It is the founding story he has told for decades, and it explains the shape of everything that followed: he has always been more interested in the systems that make discovery possible than in any single discovery.

His education was built one deliberate step at a time, almost entirely in India. He earned a bachelor's degree in physics from the University of Madras in 1981, a bachelor of engineering in electronics and communication from the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru in 1984, and a master of technology in electrical engineering from IIT Madras in 1986. Only then did he leave — for the University of Ottawa in Canada, where he completed his PhD in electrical and computer engineering in 1989, working on algorithms for image coding. The sequence matters to his story: unlike the single-degree emigrant, Panchanathan arrived in North America as a fully formed Indian-trained engineer, and he has spent his career arguing that the two systems strengthen each other.

The researcher: computing that helps people see, move and connect

He stayed at Ottawa as a professor, founding its Visual Computing and Communications Laboratory and working on the image and video compression science behind the JPEG and MPEG standards. In 1997 he moved to Arizona State University in Tempe, where he has now spent 28 years.

His own research settled into a distinctive field: human-centred computing, and in particular technology for people with disabilities. In 2001 — the same year he became a full professor and an IEEE Fellow — he founded ASU's Center for Cognitive Ubiquitous Computing (CUbiC), which built assistive systems including technology to help people who are blind or visually impaired navigate and understand their surroundings. The work won him Arizona's Governor's Innovator of the Year Award for Academia in 2004 and runs through his later honours: India's Padma Shri citation in 2025 also singled out his contributions to technologies that improve quality of life for people with disabilities. Across his career he has published more than 485 scholarly papers and mentored more than 150 graduate students, postdoctoral researchers and scientists, according to the NSF and ASU.

The builder: tripling a university's research engine

What turned Panchanathan from a successful professor into a national figure was institution-building. He founded and led ASU's School of Computing and Informatics and its Department of Biomedical Informatics, then rose through the university's research leadership: chief research officer in 2009, head of the Office of Knowledge Enterprise Development in 2011, and executive vice president of the ASU Knowledge Enterprise and chief research and innovation officer in 2016. Under his leadership ASU's research volume tripled, research expenditures reached $635 million by 2018, and the university was repeatedly named the most innovative in the United States by U.S. News & World Report.

"Panch is one of the most remarkable systems thinkers we have in this country," ASU President Michael M. Crow said when the Bueche Award was announced. "When big problems need to be solved, Panch needs to be in the room." It is telling that Panchanathan was nominated for the Bueche Award by Suresh Garimella, president of the University of Arizona — ASU's fiercest athletic rival, and another Indian-born engineer leading an American research university.

Running American science: the NSF years

Washington noticed early. In 2014, President Barack Obama appointed Panchanathan to the National Science Board, the NSF's governing body — making him, according to the American Bazaar, the first Indian American to serve on it. In December 2019, President Donald Trump nominated him as NSF director. The Senate confirmed him unanimously on June 18, 2020, and he took office on June 23 — in the middle of a pandemic, with American laboratories shut or scrambling and the race for a vaccine under way.

His five-year tenure produced the most structural change at the NSF in a generation. In 2022 he launched the Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (TIP) — the agency's first new directorate in more than 30 years — built to move discoveries out of the lab and into the economy through translational research, regional innovation engines and workforce programs. His NSF stood up a network of 27 national artificial intelligence research institutes, created the GRANTED program to broaden participation in research, and launched a Global Centers program for large international collaborations. He also championed formal research partnerships with India, connecting NSF-backed researchers with India's Department of Science and Technology and its Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology in fields including artificial intelligence, data science and advanced wireless.

He resigned on April 24, 2025, writing that he had done all he could to advance the agency's mission and that it was time to pass the baton — a departure that came as the White House proposed cutting the NSF budget by more than half. He left as the rare science chief to have served under three presidents across both parties.

"I'm honored and humbled by this recognition. Awards like this are never only about the individual. They are about the scores of people that have contributed to the outcomes recognized."

— Sethuraman Panchanathan, on receiving the Bueche Award

Two countries, two of their highest honours

The honours have arrived from both directions. Panchanathan was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 2024, among the highest distinctions for an American engineer. On May 27, 2025, President Droupadi Murmu conferred the Padma Shri on him in New Delhi, one of India's highest civilian awards, recognising a career spanning research, higher education, innovation and government leadership. IIT Madras has named him a Distinguished Alumnus. The Bueche Award now completes a pairing no Indian-born scientist had achieved before him: top civilian recognition in India and engineering's top policy honour in the United States, in consecutive years.

What he is doing now — and why the diaspora should watch

Panchanathan is back at ASU as University Professor of Technology and Innovation and Foundation Chair in Computing and Augmented Intelligence, working on artificial intelligence, quantum computing and the future of higher education in the AI era. In April 2026, Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego appointed him to lead the city's quantum strategy — a sign that his policy career did not end with the NSF. He is married, with two children and three grandchildren.

For Indian engineers and students, his arc is the argument he has made in every job: where you start is not the ceiling. A boy from Chennai who collected degrees from Madras, Bengaluru and Ottawa, who built his reputation on technology for people the tech industry usually overlooks, ended up deciding how the United States funds science itself — and used the job to wire American and Indian research closer together. The Bueche Award's 43-year wait for an Indian American winner is over. The systems he built to widen the door behind him are the part of his record most likely to outlast the medal.
